c.text: Chapter 1 – Called, Not Qualified
The feeling you’re having is normal
Someone asked you to lead.

Maybe it was the pastor, maybe a ministry head, maybe nobody asked at all and the need was simply sitting there until you picked it up. Either way, you said yes, and somewhere between saying yes and this moment, a quiet thought arrived:
They’ve made a mistake.
I’m not the right person for this.
I want to tell you something before we go one step further.

Feeling inadequate does not, by itself, mean you were wrongly chosen. Several leaders in Scripture voiced serious doubts when God called them. Their stories invite us to bring our doubts to God and seek help, rather than treating confidence as the test of a calling.
Moses argued for a full chapter and a half

In Exodus 3, Moses is eighty years old and keeping sheep in Midian. He is not a rising leader. He is a man who tried to help his people forty years earlier, killed an Egyptian, panicked, and ran. He has been in the desert ever since, working for his father-in-law.

God speaks to him from a burning bush and tells him to go to Pharaoh and bring Israel out of Egypt. Moses answers in Exodus 3:11 by asking who he is that he should go to Pharaoh. That is objection number one, and he is only getting started. He goes on to ask what he should say if they want to know God’s name (3:13), to insist that they will not believe him (4:1), to protest that he is not a good speaker and never has been (4:10), and finally to simply ask God to send somebody else (4:13).
Five objections.
God answers four of them patiently and gets angry at the fifth – not because Moses felt inadequate, but because Moses used his inadequacy as a reason to refuse.
Notice what God never does.

He never tells Moses he is wrong about himself. He never says, “Actually, you’re an excellent speaker.” He answers a completely different question. In Exodus 3:12 he says simply that he will be with him. The issue was never Moses’ capacity. It was God’s presence.
Jeremiah felt too young, and God answered him

The same pattern appears in Jeremiah 1:6. Jeremiah objects that he cannot speak because he is young; the passage does not give his exact age. He was called to prophesy in Judah in the decades before Jerusalem fell to Babylon, an assignment that would bring rejection, imprisonment and danger.

God’s reply in verses 7 and 8 is not encouragement about Jeremiah’s hidden potential. It is a redirection: don’t say you’re too young, go where I send you, say what I tell you, don’t be afraid of their faces, because I am with you.
Again – presence, not capacity.
The disciples were “unschooled, ordinary men”

Acts 4:13 describes the moment the Sanhedrin – the trained religious elite of Jerusalem – watch Peter and John speak with confidence and realise these are uneducated, ordinary men. The Greek word behind “unschooled” refers to someone without formal rabbinic training. These were fishermen standing in front of the theological faculty of their nation.
The verse ends with the detail that matters: the council recognised that they had been with Jesus.
Their time with Jesus mattered.
They had learned from him, and their courage was not dependent on elite credentials. That does not make training unnecessary; it reminds us that formal status is not the whole measure of a leader.
So what does God actually ask of a leader?
Here is where new leaders can get the emphasis wrong.
We may look first for impressive ability, while Paul’s instructions give sustained attention to character, maturity and the ability to teach and care for others.
Read 1 Timothy 3:1-7 slowly.

Paul is addressing the qualifications of overseers. He describes a person of sound character: faithful, self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, free from greed and respected beyond the church. He also requires teaching ability, maturity and responsible care of the household. These are substantial responsibilities, not a call to appoint anyone who is willing.
Character is central, but capability is not absent.
These requirements address overseers specifically; churches should also define the character, training and competence needed for each volunteer role.
Then look at 1 Corinthians 1:26-29.

Paul is writing to a church in a wealthy, status-obsessed port city, and he reminds them to look at themselves – not many of them were wise by human standards, not many were influential, not many were of noble birth. God chose what the world considers foolish and weak, Paul says, precisely so that no one could stand in front of him and boast.
Your uncertainty can keep you teachable.
It should also help you identify the preparation and support you need.
The one thing you cannot borrow

There is a line in 2 Corinthians 3:5-6 that I would encourage you to memorise this week. Paul says that he is not competent in himself to claim anything as coming from him; his competence comes from God, who has made him a minister of a new covenant.
Paul, trained under Gamaliel and deeply familiar with the Scriptures, still recognises that his ministry depends on God.

If that is true of Paul, the pressure you are feeling to be enough is a pressure God never put on you. You cannot borrow someone else’s gifting, and you do not need to. What you need is a real, daily, ongoing connection to the One who called you. That is the subject of the next chapter, and it is not an accident that it comes second.
What “called” does and does not mean
Two cautions before we close.
First, calling is not the same as feeling certain.

Many new leaders wait for a supernatural confirmation before they will commit. That is not the usual pattern. More often the call arrives as a need you can see, a nudge you cannot shake, and the confirmation of people who know you. If your pastor and your church see something in you, take that seriously – God frequently speaks through the body before he speaks in your emotions.
Second, calling is not permission to stay as you are.

God did not require Moses to be qualified, but he did require him to go. Character is what God asks for, and character grows. You will need to learn things you do not know yet. This guide exists because leadership has real skills attached to it – running a meeting, recruiting a volunteer, handling a critic – and being called does not download those skills into you.
You are not required to be ready. You are required to be willing, teachable, and honest about what you do not know.
That is a sound place to begin learning. It is not permission to bypass the training, supervision or safeguarding requirements of the role.
